transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, um... I suppose occupational health sent me. They’ve been hovering a lot lately, ever since the university brought in the new compliance officer. He’s absolutely obsessed with everyone taking their mandated breaks, which—if you know anything about biological sciences—is just not how the real world works. You can't exactly tell a live cell culture to pause and wait for you while you go down to the cafeteria, you know? 

But anyway, they flagged me because I’ve gotten into this pattern where I just... push breakfast and lunch aside during my lab runs. Or during my exhibition work. We’re actually setting up this massive marine microbiology exhibit right now for the public, and the bioluminescent algae are incredibly finicky. If the ambient temperature fluctuates even a single degree, the whole tank just goes completely dark, so I've been practically living in the observation room making sure the chillers are calibrated. 

So because of all that, I just push meals off, and then by the time I finally do eat, I keep it to something very small and controlled. It’s just more efficient that way, really.

Outside of work and your responsibilities in the lab or with the exhibit, how have things been for you emotionally or in your daily life? Have you noticed any changes in how you feel or function when you’re not at the lab?

Well, emotionally... I mean, I'm functioning fine in terms of the work itself. I'm still hitting all the major deadlines for the exhibit, which is a miracle considering the supply chain issues we've had with the specialized acrylic for the tanks. Do you know how hard it is to source marine-grade acrylic right now? It's practically impossible because of some backlog at the manufacturing plant in Germany, so we've had to use this temporary sealant that smells absolutely awful. 

But, um, I guess outside of the actual work... I don't really do much else anymore. I used to go to the lab lunches, or those informal planning dinners we'd have for the gallery space, but I just stopped going. It's too complicated to sit there while everyone is ordering heavy food and expecting you to do the same. So I just stay behind in the lab. It's quieter anyway. But I suppose it does mean I'm a lot more isolated from my colleagues than I used to be. Not that they really understand the algae anyway, to be honest. Most of them are more focused on the macro-biology side of things, like the coral reef structures, which is fascinating, sure, but it doesn't have the same delicate balance as the microorganisms.
Have you noticed that you don’t enjoy things as much as you used to, or that you’ve lost interest in activities you once found pleasurable?

Well, um... I don't think I've lost interest in things, really. I mean, the exhibit is still fascinating to me. It's just that I don't really have time for anything else right now. Although, to be fair, I did used to really enjoy hiking on the weekends. There's this trail just outside the city—have you ever been to the Pine Ridge reserve? It's absolutely stunning in the autumn. The way the light filters through the canopy... it's just incredible. 

But I haven't been in months. Partly because of the exhibit, obviously, but also... I just don't really have the energy for it anymore. Which is a shame, because I used to collect the most amazing lichen samples out there. Lichen is actually incredibly resilient, you know. It can survive in the most extreme environments. There was this one study where they exposed it to the vacuum of space, and it just... went dormant and then revived when they brought it back. It's fascinating how organisms adapt to deprivation like that. But anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, right, enjoying things. Yeah, I don't know. I guess I just don't really do much besides work anymore.
Have you been feeling down or depressed most days, even when you're not at work or thinking about the exhibit?

Well, depressed? Um... I don't really think so. I mean, not depressed, just... tired, I suppose. But speaking of being down, the basement level where the lab is located is incredibly depressing, architecturally speaking. It's this brutalist concrete bunker from the 1970s. They actually used to house the electron microscopes down there because it's the most vibrationally stable part of the building, which makes sense, but they painted the walls this awful, institutional seafoam green. 

I've been trying to get facilities to let us repaint it white, or at least put in some full-spectrum lighting, because right now it feels like you're working inside a submarine. Have you ever read about the psychological effects of submarine deployments on naval crews? It's fascinating how the lack of natural light completely disrupts their circadian rhythms. They have to use these specialized lighting schedules just to keep people from losing their minds. 

But anyway... no, I wouldn't say I feel depressed most days. Just focused on the work, really. And maybe a bit drained from dealing with the facilities management office. They are notoriously difficult to get ahold of.
Outside of the stressors related to work and the exhibit, do you find yourself feeling down or low in your day-to-day life, even when things aren’t particularly stressful?

Um... no, I don't think so. When things aren't stressful, I guess I feel perfectly fine. It's just rare that things aren't stressful right now. But when I do have a quiet moment at home, I'm usually just focused on my plants. I've been trying to cultivate these Maidenhair ferns in my living room, and they are notoriously finicky about ambient humidity. 

I actually ended up building this automated misting system using a Raspberry Pi microcontroller just to keep them from dying. It was a fun little distraction, honestly. You have to keep the humidity exactly around 60 percent, otherwise the fronds just crisp up and drop overnight. Did you know that ferns reproduce via spores rather than seeds? It's a completely different evolutionary mechanism. They have this intermediate stage called a prothallus that is incredibly vulnerable to desiccation. It's fascinating how ancient their reproductive cycle is compared to flowering plants. They've been around since before the dinosaurs, which really puts our modern problems into perspective if you think about it. 

But, um... sorry, what was the question? Oh, feeling low. No, I wouldn't say I feel low. Just... busy trying to keep everything functioning, I suppose.
Have you noticed that you don’t take as much pleasure in things as you used to, even outside of work or the lab?

I mean, I don't really think so? Like I said, I still enjoy my plants and... well, I guess I haven't been doing much else. But I still find things interesting. Oh, actually, speaking of the ferns, I was reading this article the other night about how certain species of fungi form these symbiotic relationships with plant roots—mycorrhizal networks, they're called. It's basically an underground communication system. The fungi help the plants absorb nutrients, and in return, the plants give the fungi carbohydrates. 

Some researchers even think trees use these networks to send distress signals to each other if they're being attacked by insects. It's like a botanical internet! I was thinking about trying to introduce some beneficial mycorrhizae to my potted plants to see if it improves their resilience, but you have to be really careful about sourcing the right spores, otherwise you could just end up introducing a pathogen by mistake. The delicate balance of micro-ecosystems is just so easy to disrupt. 

But um, wait, pleasure in things? Yeah, no, I think I still enjoy things just fine. I just get caught up in my projects, you know?
Have you noticed that you don’t take as much pleasure in things as you used to, even outside of work or the lab?

Wait, didn't you just ask me that? Or... sorry, maybe I didn't actually give you a straight answer a second ago. No, I really don't think I've lost pleasure in things. Like I was saying, I still have my hobbies and my plants. 

Actually, besides the ferns, I've recently started paying a lot of attention to the urban wildlife outside my apartment window. There's a family of crows nesting near my fire escape, and corvids are just remarkably intelligent. Did you know they can recognize individual human faces? There was this famous study at the University of Washington where researchers wore these rubber caveman masks while banding the birds, and for years afterward, the crows would scold anyone walking around campus in that specific mask. They even taught their offspring to recognize the masks, which is just a phenomenal example of cultural transmission in a non-human species. It completely changes how you think about animal cognition. 

I've actually been experimenting with leaving out little shiny pieces of metal on the windowsill to see if they'll bring me gifts in return, since they're known to do that in urban environments. They completely ignored the copper wire I left out yesterday, but they seem to really respond to aluminum tabs... 

But, right, sorry. I'm doing it again. The point is, no, I still enjoy things just fine. I definitely haven't lost interest in the world around me.
Looking back over the past few months, have you found that activities you used to enjoy, like hiking or collecting lichen, no longer give you the same sense of pleasure or satisfaction?

Um... no, not really. I don't think I've lost the pleasure in those things. I still love the idea of hiking and going out to collect lichen. It's just that I haven't had the time or energy to actually get out to the woods lately. 

Speaking of lichen, though, I was actually reading this fascinating paper the other day about how they aren't just a simple symbiosis between a fungus and an algae like we were all taught in school. It turns out, a lot of them actually have a third partner—a specific type of yeast that's embedded in the cortex. It completely upended decades of established lichenology! The researchers only found it because they were doing genetic sequencing and kept getting these weird anomalous results that didn't match the known fungal or algal DNA. It just goes to show how much we still don't know about these micro-ecosystems that are literally growing on every tree and rock around us. I've been meaning to get out my hand lens and look closer at the *Parmelia* growing on the oak tree down my street to see if I can spot any morphological differences that might hint at that third partner. 

But um, yeah, to answer your question, I still enjoy those things. I just haven't been doing them as much.
Looking back, would you say that you no longer feel the same joy or excitement when you think about things like hiking or collecting lichen, even when you're not focused on work?

I mean, I think I just said that, right? I still feel the excitement. I still love the idea of it. It's not the joy that's missing, it's just... well, the physical exhaustion, honestly. 

But you know, thinking about hiking reminds me of this trail I used to do up in the Cascades. The elevation gain was brutal, but the alpine flora was just incredible once you got above the tree line. There's this one specific plant, *Silene acaulis*, moss campion—it grows in these tight little cushion shapes to protect itself from the freezing wind and retain moisture. It's a brilliant evolutionary adaptation to extreme environments. The inside of the cushion can actually be significantly warmer than the ambient air temperature. I remember sitting there on this freezing ridge, just staring at this tiny pink flower, thinking about how much energy it takes just to survive in those conditions, let alone bloom. It really makes you appreciate the sheer tenacity of biological life, you know? They can live for hundreds of years, just slowly expanding millimeter by millimeter over the rocks. 

But um... yeah. I definitely still get excited about that stuff. I'm just... not doing it right now.

When you think about hiking or collecting lichen, even if you don’t have the time or energy to do it now, do you still feel the same sense of anticipation or emotional reward just from thinking about it?

I feel like we're going in circles a bit, doctor. But yes, absolutely. I still feel that same anticipation. Just thinking about finding a rare specimen or getting back out on the trail gets me excited. 

You know, anticipation itself is such a fascinating biological mechanism when you really look at it. Even organisms without central nervous systems exhibit it. Have you ever read about *Physarum polycephalum*? The true slime molds? They're incredible. They don't have a brain, not a single neuron, but they can actually anticipate periodic environmental changes. There was this brilliant experiment where researchers exposed a slime mold to cold, dry conditions at very specific, regular intervals. After a few rounds, the slime mold actually started slowing down its growth in *anticipation* of the next cold shock, exactly on schedule, even when the researchers stopped applying the cold! It's this primitive, non-neural cellular memory. It completely redefines what we consider "learning" or "memory" in biology. I actually have a small culture of it in a petri dish in my lab right now, and watching it map out the most efficient routes to find oat flakes is just... it's mesmerizing. 

But, right. Sorry. I know I'm doing it again. To answer your question, yes, I still get an emotional reward from my hobbies. I promise I haven't lost that. I'm just too physically exhausted to go out and do them right now.

When you think about things you used to enjoy, like hiking or collecting lichen, do you still feel any emotional pleasure or satisfaction from the thought itself, even if you aren't actually doing them right now?

I... Doctor, I really feel like I've answered this exact question three times now. Yes. I still feel the pleasure. I still feel the satisfaction just thinking about it. The joy is there. 

It's actually kind of funny we keep coming back to this, because it reminds me of this behavioral loop I was studying in *Drosophila*—fruit flies—back in grad school. We were looking at how they process repetitive stimuli. If you present them with the exact same olfactory cue over and over, eventually they just habituate to it. The sensory neurons literally stop firing as strongly because the brain decides the information is no longer novel or useful. It's a way to conserve metabolic energy, right? Why waste ATP processing a signal that isn't changing? But if you alter the concentration even slightly, or pair it with a mild electric shock, suddenly the whole neural pathway lights up again. It's fascinating how the brain filters out redundancy. 

But um, yes. The answer is still yes. I still get pleasure from thinking about my hobbies.
Do you find that you no longer feel pleasure or satisfaction, even in small, everyday moments that used to make you happy, like seeing a familiar plant bloom or hearing a favorite song?

Okay, I really don't mean to be difficult, doctor, but are you just reading down a list of variations of the exact same question? Because my answer hasn't changed. No. I haven't lost the ability to feel happy about small things. Seeing a plant bloom still brings me a lot of joy. 

Actually, since you specifically brought up blooming... it's funny you mention that, because the molecular mechanism behind how a plant actually "knows" when to bloom is incredible. Most people just think, oh, it gets warm, so the flowers open. But it's actually about the photoperiod. They are literally measuring the length of the dark period, the night. There's this photoreceptor protein in the leaves—phytochrome—that acts like a molecular light switch. When the days get long enough, it triggers the expression of this specific gene, *FLOWERING LOCUS T*. And the resulting protein actually travels all the way from the leaf, through the phloem, up to the shoot apex to tell the plant to make a flower instead of just another leaf. It's a literal chemical message traveling through the plant's vascular system. 

I spent a whole semester in my undergrad just tracking that protein movement in *Arabidopsis thaliana*. We used these fluorescent markers, so under the microscope, you could actually see this glowing green signal migrating through the tissue. It was like watching a tiny highway light up at night. I could spend hours just looking at those slides. 

So... yeah. I definitely still feel satisfaction. I haven't lost that spark for the things I love, big or small. The pleasure is completely intact, I promise.
Even if you still intellectually enjoy the idea of your hobbies, have you noticed that actually engaging in them—when you do get the chance—doesn’t feel as rewarding or pleasurable as it used to?

Doctor, I... okay. Honestly, I don't know how else to say this. I feel like I'm taking a pop quiz where I keep giving the right answer but the professor keeps rephrasing the question hoping I'll get it wrong. No. When I actually do get the chance to engage in them, it still feels rewarding. I haven't noticed any drop in the pleasure of actually doing the things I love. 

It's just the energy, you know? It's like... well, it's like cellular respiration. You can have all the glucose in the world, all the potential energy just sitting there waiting to be used, but if you don't have the oxygen to act as the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain, the whole system just grinds to a halt. The potential is there, the desire is there, the mechanism is perfectly intact, but the ATP just isn't being produced. 

I remember when I first really understood the Krebs cycle—not just memorized it for a test, but actually visualized it. It was during a late-night study session in the library, and it just clicked. This beautiful, elegant cycle of enzymes and substrates, constantly turning, constantly generating energy. It's so perfectly balanced. If just one enzyme is inhibited, like if you introduce fluoroacetate—which is actually found in some poisonous plants in Australia, fascinating defense mechanism—it completely blocks aconitase, and the whole cycle stops. The organism literally starves at a cellular level, even with abundant nutrients. 

But, um, anyway. No. The reward is the same. The pleasure is the same. I just don't have the energy to do it right now.
Have you noticed a persistent lack of energy or fatigue that doesn't seem to be related to how much sleep you've had or how hard you've been working?

No, I haven't noticed anything like that. If I'm tired, it's because I didn't sleep well or I've been on my feet in the lab all day. It's not some mysterious, unexplained fatigue. 

Speaking of sleep, though, it's actually incredible how the biological clock works even when you're completely exhausted. Have you ever looked into the circadian rhythms of cyanobacteria? We worked with *Synechococcus elongatus* for a while. They have this core oscillator made of just three proteins—KaiA, KaiB, and KaiC. You can literally extract them, put them in a test tube with some ATP, and they will maintain a perfect 24-hour rhythm of phosphorylation all by themselves, completely *in vitro*. No living cell required. It’s just a chemical clock ticking away in a tube. 

I remember watching the assay results come in at like 3 AM one night. I was completely sleep-deprived, drinking that awful acidic coffee from the department breakroom, and just marveling at how these extracted proteins had a better grasp of time than I did. My own circadian rhythm was completely destroyed that year. I used to keep a sleeping bag under my desk because the time points for the assays were so strict. You'd just crash for two hours, wake up to your alarm, pipette your samples, and go back to sleep on the floor. 

But, um... wait, what were we just talking about? Oh, right, the fatigue thing. No, I don't have that. If I'm exhausted, there's a logical reason for it.
Looking back over the past two weeks, have you found that you don’t take pleasure in things you used to enjoy, even when you’re not at work or thinking about the lab?

I just... I don't know why we're still stuck on this. I really don't. No, I haven't lost pleasure in things outside the lab. I still enjoy my life. 

Actually, speaking of being outside the lab, I was walking through the botanical gardens this weekend—which I still very much enjoy, by the way—and they had this whole section on carnivorous plants. It's fascinating how they evolved to survive in nutrient-poor soil. Like the Venus flytrap, *Dionaea muscipula*. People think it's just this simple mechanical trap, but it's actually an electrical system. When an insect touches the trigger hairs on the inside of the leaf, it generates an action potential, similar to what happens in human neurons. But it doesn't snap shut right away. The plant actually counts. It waits for a second touch within about twenty seconds to confirm it's actually prey and not just a raindrop or a piece of debris. It's an incredible energy-saving mechanism, because closing that trap and secreting digestive enzymes takes a massive amount of ATP. 

I remember reading this paper in grad school where they actually attached tiny electrodes to the traps to measure the voltage changes. They could artificially trigger it with electrical pulses. It's just wild to think about plants having a primitive sort of memory and electrical signaling network. 

So, yeah. I still find plenty of things enjoyable and fascinating, whether I'm at work or not. I'm not sitting around feeling miserable and empty, I promise you.
When you engage in small, everyday moments—like seeing a plant bloom or hearing a familiar bird call—do you feel the same emotional pleasure and satisfaction as you used to?

Yes, absolutely. I still feel the exact same satisfaction. I mean, I really do. 

You mentioned bird calls, and honestly, that's one of my favorite things to pay attention to. Did you know that songbirds don't actually have a larynx like we do? They have a syrinx, which is located way down at the base of their trachea, right where it branches into the lungs. It's an incredibly efficient acoustic mechanism. They have near one hundred percent efficiency in converting airflow into sound, whereas human vocal cords are at like... maybe two percent on a good day. 

I had a colleague in grad school who studied bioacoustics, specifically looking at how urban noise pollution is forcing city birds to sing at higher frequencies just to be heard over low-frequency traffic rumble. We used to sit on the roof of the biology building at dawn with this massive parabolic microphone, recording robins and sparrows. When you run the audio through a spectrogram, you can actually see the pitch shift compared to rural populations. It's behavioral adaptation, maybe even rapid evolution, happening right in front of us. 

And the most amazing part is that some species can actually control the two halves of their syrinx independently. They're essentially singing a complex duet with themselves. Wood thrushes do that, and the harmonic complexity is just... well, it's breathtaking. You can't help but feel a sense of wonder when you really understand the mechanics of what you're hearing.

So... wait, yes. To answer your question, when I hear something like that, or see a plant bloom, I absolutely still feel the same emotional pleasure. It's still completely fascinating and satisfying to me. I haven't lost that at all.
Have you noticed any difficulty concentrating or staying focused, even when you're working on tasks you find interesting or important?

No, I haven't noticed any trouble concentrating. I mean, my work requires intense focus, and I can still do it just fine. 

Actually, speaking of focus, it's really interesting how the brain manages attention, especially on a neurochemical level. We were looking into some literature recently on the locus coeruleus, this tiny nucleus in the pons. It's the primary source of norepinephrine in the brain. When you're engaged in a task, the locus coeruleus fires in this very specific phasic mode—it's like a focused burst of activity that optimizes your attention to the relevant stimuli and filters out distractions. 

But what's really wild is what happens when you're stressed or when the task goes on too long. The firing pattern shifts from phasic to tonic. It just starts firing constantly, at a baseline level, and that's when you get distractible. Your brain is basically scanning the environment for new, more rewarding stimuli. It's an evolutionary mechanism to keep us from getting stuck on a dead-end task, but in a modern lab setting, it just means you suddenly find yourself organizing your pipette tips by color instead of running your gels. 

I actually had a colleague who tried to hack his own locus coeruleus function using various nootropics to maintain that phasic firing state during a massive grant-writing push. I told him he was just going to downregulate his receptors, but you know how people get when a deadline is looming. He ended up crashing so hard he slept for like two days straight after submission. 

But, um... anyway. My concentration is fine. I can still focus on my work without any issues.
Have you noticed that you don’t take as much pleasure in things as you used to, even outside of work or the lab?

I feel like we just talked about this. No, I haven't lost pleasure in things. I really haven't. 

I was actually just reading this fascinating article about dopamine pathways and how they relate to the anticipation of reward versus the actual consumption of the reward. It's so interesting because people always think of dopamine as the "pleasure" chemical, but it's actually much more about motivation and wanting. The actual hedonic pleasure—the "liking" part—is mediated more by opioid and endocannabinoid hotspots in the brain, like in the nucleus accumbens shell. 

There was this classic experiment by Kent Berridge where they depleted dopamine in rats. The rats wouldn't seek out food at all—they had zero motivation, they'd literally starve if you didn't put food directly into their mouths. But when the researchers did put something sweet in their mouths, the rats still showed the exact same positive facial expressions, the same lip-licking responses as normal rats. They still *liked* the reward, they just didn't *want* it enough to work for it. It completely upended how neuroscientists thought about the reward system. 

It makes you think about how we structure our whole lives around seeking things, assuming the getting will feel good, but the brain is actually running two completely different chemical circuits for the wanting and the liking. It's why you can crave something intensely, but then when you get it, it's just... meh. Or vice versa. 

Anyway... no. I still enjoy things just fine. My pleasure in things hasn't changed.
Have you noticed that, even when you do engage in things you used to enjoy, you don’t feel the same emotional response or warmth toward them—like they feel more mechanical or empty than they used to?

No, they don't feel empty. I don't... I don't feel like my emotional response is mechanical at all. 

It's funny you use the word "mechanical," though, because I was just talking to a postdoc in the engineering department about biomechanics, specifically regarding insect flight. It is absolutely wild. For a long time, aerodynamicists couldn't figure out how bumblebees could fly, because according to fixed-wing aerodynamic theory, they shouldn't be able to generate enough lift. Their wings are too small for their body mass. 

But it turns out, insect wings don't work like airplane wings. They don't just flap up and down; they rotate. They create these leading-edge vortices—little tornadoes of air that sit right on top of the wing and create this massive low-pressure zone that essentially sucks the bug upward. The mechanics of it are so incredibly precise and complex. And the flight muscles! In flies and bees, the muscles don't even contract in direct response to a nerve impulse for every single flap. They have asynchronous muscles, where one contraction stretches the opposing muscle, which triggers *that* muscle to contract, creating this rapid oscillation. A nerve impulse just sort of turns the system on and off, but the mechanical resonance of the thorax takes over. It's like plucking a guitar string. 

We were actually looking at some high-speed camera footage of hawkmoths hovering, and the way their wings deform and twist under the aerodynamic load is just beautiful. It's fluid dynamics and structural engineering perfectly evolved. You look at something like that, and "mechanical" stops being a cold word and becomes something... well, something miraculous. 

But, right, to your question. No, I don't feel empty or mechanical about the things I enjoy. I still feel the same warmth toward them.
Have you experienced any days where you felt down or low, even when nothing particularly stressful or negative was happening?

No, I don't think so. I don't really have days where I just feel down for no reason. 

Although, speaking of feeling low, we were actually looking at some data recently on how light exposure affects mood and circadian rhythms, specifically the melanopsin-expressing retinal ganglion cells. It's fascinating because these cells don't even contribute to image-forming vision—they're just there to measure ambient light intensity and tell the suprachiasmatic nucleus what time of day it is. 

But what's really interesting is that these cells project directly to the perihabenular nucleus, which is a brain region involved in mood regulation. So there's this direct, hardwired anatomical pathway from your eyes to your mood centers that has nothing to do with what you're actually looking at, just the quality and intensity of the light. It's why shift work or being stuck in a windowless lab all day can be so detrimental. 

We had this one tech in the lab who bought one of those massive 10,000 lux therapy lamps and just blasted it at her face while she was doing data analysis. She swore it made her more productive, but honestly, I think it just gave her a headache. She ended up putting it on a timer so it would mimic a natural sunrise, which is a much better way to entrain your circadian clock anyway. The sudden onset of bright light can actually cause a phase delay if you time it wrong, which just makes everything worse. 

But, um... no. I don't have days where I just feel down out of nowhere. My mood is fine.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences distress or impairment outside of work-related contexts, which would help differentiate between adjustment disorder (F43.20) and other candidates like eating disorder (F50.00) or unspecified insomnia (F51.80).
doctor.question: Outside of work and your responsibilities in the lab or with the exhibit, how have things been for you emotionally or in your daily life? Have you noticed any changes in how you feel or function when you’re not at the lab?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still meeting the main deadlines, but I’ve stopped going to lab lunches and informal gallery planning meals, so I’m more isolated from colleagues than I used to be.

patient.answer:
Well, emotionally... I mean, I'm functioning fine in terms of the work itself. I'm still hitting all the major deadlines for the exhibit, which is a miracle considering the supply chain issues we've had with the specialized acrylic for the tanks. Do you know how hard it is to source marine-grade acrylic right now? It's practically impossible because of some backlog at the manufacturing plant in Germany, so we've had to use this temporary sealant that smells absolutely awful. 

But, um, I guess outside of the actual work... I don't really do much else anymore. I used to go to the lab lunches, or those informal planning dinners we'd have for the gallery space, but I just stopped going. It's too complicated to sit there while everyone is ordering heavy food and expecting you to do the same. So I just stay behind in the lab. It's quieter anyway. But I suppose it does mean I'm a lot more isolated from my colleagues than I used to be. Not that they really understand the algae anyway, to be honest. Most of them are more focused on the macro-biology side of things, like the coral reef structures, which is fascinating, sure, but it doesn't have the same delicate balance as the microorganisms.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a loss of pleasure or interest in activities they previously enjoyed, to help differentiate between depression and other conditions.
doctor.question: Have you noticed that you don’t enjoy things as much as you used to, or that you’ve lost interest in activities you once found pleasurable?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about anhedonia or loss of interest in pleasurable activities (symptoms of depression), which is not covered by any of the provided symptom profiles for Anorexia Nervosa.

patient.answer:
Well, um... I don't think I've lost interest in things, really. I mean, the exhibit is still fascinating to me. It's just that I don't really have time for anything else right now. opening_question.intent: Identify the patient's primary concern or reason for seeking help
opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent patterns of restrictive eating and weight loss behaviors, primarily driven by a strong focus on control and efficiency rather than body image concerns. There is clear evidence of significant social withdrawal and reduced engagement in previously enjoyed activities, yet the patient denies loss of pleasure (anhedonia) and reports intact emotional engagement with interests. The absence of depressed mood, anhedonia, and presence of restrictive eating behaviors point away from major depressive disorder (F32.90) and adjustment disorder (F43.20) and more toward a non-organic eating disorder, specifically Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID), which is coded as F50.00.
